POST /api/entry is idempotent by design (issue #9), so every extra gate submission answers with the same opening sentence. enter() had no re-entrancy guard, the gate stayed live until the response returned, and showPersona APPENDED. On a wired deployment the assignment is a Snowflake checkout plus a roster read, so the window is seconds wide and a held Enter key or a double tap fills it. FoundryConfig gains timeout_seconds (default 90.0) and max_retries (default 1), read from CHIP_CHAT_FOUNDRY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS and CHIP_CHAT_FOUNDRY_MAX_RETRIES, and both are passed explicitly to BOTH AzureOpenAI constructions in chat_client -- the api-key path and the Entra path. Two constructions in one function is exactly where a keyword gets added to the first and forgotten on the second, and the forgotten one would have been Entra, which is the path production takes; a test asserts both.

max_retries is one rather than the library's two because retries multiply against the timeout AND the step count, and because the deployment's observed failure mode under concurrency is RateLimitError from a gpt-5-mini at capacity 10 (docs/deployment.md section 3.13) -- a third attempt into a deployment refusing for want of capacity spends ninety more seconds to be told the same thing. It is set explicitly rather than left to the default so the number is a decision somebody made and can find, which is the whole reason this bug existed.

An unreadable value is REFUSED rather than ignored. Somebody who writes CHIP_CHAT_FOUNDRY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=90s believes they have set a timeout; falling back to the default would leave them believing it, which is the original bug in a new costume. Five parametrised cases cover it.

DELIBERATELY NOT A TURN BUDGET, and the code and the doc both say so. A turn is up to DEFAULT_MAX_STEPS calls, so the worst case is the per-call bound times the attempts times the steps. One test computes that figure rather than asserting a constant, so it reports the real number whenever either constant moves, and fails if it creeps back towards an hour. Bounding the turn is a separate mechanism that was not built, because it has to decide what the assistant SAYS when it fires -- whether the partial answer goes out, whether the tool results so far are worth anything -- and that is a product decision rather than an HTTP client setting.

Nine tests in agent/tests/test_model_call_timeout.py; docs/decisions/model-call-timeout.md is the record.

NOT MEASURED, and the docstring, the decision record and the test file all say so: whether ninety seconds is the right number. docs/deployment.md section 3.13 measured p50 41 s, p95 72.8 s and a longest of 95.2 s, but those are WHOLE TURNS -- several calls plus tool time -- and nothing in this repository has measured a single completion in isolation. Ninety is set above the longest observed whole turn on the argument that one call outlasting an entire slow conversation is a hang rather than a slow answer. That is the weakest part of the change and it is labelled as an argument, not a measurement. What would settle it: llm.completion span durations off Application Insights, which the span vocabulary already records and nobody has queried for this. Also unmeasured: how often it will fire, and what the visitor sees when it does.
